title: Proof pages for an education product
metaTitle: Education product case study page structure
excerpt: Show the constraint, the decision, and the learning moment. End on how a similar teacher or parent can start a class or a trial.

faqs.question: What belongs at the top of a proof page?
faqs.answer: The constraint, then the decision, then the learning moment. A classroom photo and a quote about engagement can wait, and often should be cut. The buyer should see the exercise or the teacher view before any film.

faqs.question: Can you publish student results?
faqs.answer: Only with a defined group, a duration, and permission, and only if the number is one you can explain. Skip invented proficiency gains. Privacy outranks a stronger screenshot. Blur a roster rather than ship a real class list.

faqs.question: How should the page end?
faqs.answer: With a similar buyer and the same action the rest of the site uses: start a class or start a trial. Say what the first session contains. Do not end on a funding announcement or a request to follow a social account.

markdown:
An education product case study page should show the constraint, the decision, and the learning moment, for a teacher or a parent with little time. Screenshots without a decision are decoration. End on how a similar buyer can start a class or a trial.

That is the job. A wall of smiling students, a quote about "engagement," and a badge chart do not do it. The buyer cannot tell what a learner did, or what you chose when something was hard.

## Constraint, decision, learning moment

Open with the constraint in ordinary words. A period that is forty minutes and already crowded. A parent who can supervise for ten minutes and cannot teach the skill. A tutor with six students in three different places in the same topic. A school that will not approve another login unless the first activity is obvious. The constraint is why the design was a choice rather than a preference.

Name the decision next. You put the practice before the points. You made the teacher view a list of who is stuck, not a chart of time-on-task. You let a child retry a step with a hint that explains, instead of a streak that scolds. One or two sentences. A teacher should be able to repeat them to a colleague.

Then show the learning moment. The actual screen: the sentence the child reads, the step the student tries, the three names on the teacher's list. Crop to that. If you cannot show a child, do not invent one. The product frame is enough, and it is often better. Faces of minors are a permission problem and, without the lesson, a distraction.

[Research on generative search](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.09735) found that pages with quotations, citations, and statistics were easier to surface, and that stuffing repeated phrases reduced visibility by about ten percent. A proof page already has something worth quoting: the decision, said once. Use a teacher's real words if you have permission and they describe the constraint. Do not pad the page with "learning" in every heading. One clear moment is more citable than a long boast.

## A classroom is not a testimonial slider

Unnamed stars, five identical quotes, and a carousel of school logos are not proof. They are a habit copied from software that sells to procurement. A teacher reading on a phone will not wait for the carousel. A parent will not trust a quote that could have been written by the marketing team, because many of them were.

If you have a real account, make it specific. The grade. The skill. What was awkward before. What the teacher or parent did on the first day. What the product refused to do. "We loved partnering with the team" can be deleted without losing information. "I could see three students stuck on regrouping before I walked over" cannot, if it is true and allowed.

Skip numbers you cannot stand behind. No invented proficiency gains. No "2x engagement" from a week of internal use. If a pilot had a result you may share, define the group, the duration, and what was measured, in a sentence a skeptic can finish. If you cannot define it, leave it out. The learning moment still carries the page. A fake delta will be the only thing a careful buyer remembers, and they will remember it against you.

Privacy outranks color. Do not publish a child's name, a roster, a voice, or a face without the permission your policy already requires. Blur badly rather than ship a screenshot that shows a real class list to the open web. A proof page that leaks a classroom is not a growth asset. It is an incident.

## What to show

Show the sequence a new user actually meets. The start of the activity. One hard step. The hint or the correction. The teacher's or parent's view afterward, if that view is part of the promise. Four frames can be enough. Twelve frames of every state is a manual. Link the manual from the product. Do not make the case study the manual.

Label what is the product and what is the surrounding story. A photograph of a kitchen table does not prove the reading practice. It can set the constraint, "this had to work on a phone on a couch," and then you still owe the screen. A classroom photo that hides the board does the same disservice. Context, then the decision, then stop.

Say what you cut. Public leaderboards. Timers that panic. A signup that demanded a school email before a parent could see a lesson. Cuts are the most believable part of an education case study, because every teacher has been hurt by the feature you removed. Write the cut as a decision, not as an apology.

Say the scope of the tool in the same place. One skill, one grade band, a supplement rather than a full curriculum. The proof page is where overclaim usually creeps back in, dressed as a success. Keep the boundary you wrote on the services page. If this class used only the fractions unit, do not title the page as if you taught the year.

Hanabi's public projects are a reminder of the shape, even though they are not courses. Down the Cove shows a migration with a constraint. Thomas Bewick shows a body of work made readable. Your proof page needs the same bones: what was hard, what you chose, what a person can now do. The person, here, is a learner or the adult responsible for one.

## How the page should end

End on a similar buyer and the start. "If you teach this grade and you need one activity that shows you who is stuck, start a class and use it in a single period before you decide." "If you want a short reading practice tonight and you do not want to teach the lesson yourself, start a trial." Those sentences respect the two readers. A single mushy ending, "bring our solution to your learners," respects neither.

Do not end on a badge, a funding announcement, or a request to follow a social account. The last line should be the action the rest of the site uses. Same words. Same destination. A new verb at the end of a case study feels like a different company walked in.

Point to one other proof page only when the constraint is different. A family story and a classroom story are a pair. Two classroom stories that repeat the same decision are one story with extra screenshots. Say why the next link is different, in the link itself, so they can skip it honestly.

Offer the proof to the buyer who cannot use this case. A parent reading a school story should see a line that points to the family trial, not a dead end. Routing is part of the ending. Confusion after a good story is how you waste the only attention you earned.

## Which story to publish first

Publish the story that matches the buyer you want this month. If you need teachers to try a class, lead with the period, the stuck-student list, and the start-a-class action. If you need families, lead with the ten-minute practice and the trial. A beautiful district logo with no classroom detail will attract meetings you cannot convert and will teach parents that the product is not for them.

You need permission, and you need a version of the product you still ship. A case study of a retired interface is a trap. The buyer starts a trial and meets a different product. If the UI has changed, update the frames or retire the page. Out-of-date proof is a kind of fiction.

One finished page is better than five posters. A poster is a logo, a quote, and a metric you will not define. Delete posters. Finish one argument. Put it where the homepage can point at it without embarrassment. If the homepage shows a learning moment the proof page never documents, one of them is aspirational. Fix that before you write a second story.

Keep the writing short enough to finish on a phone. Constraint, decision, moment, what you cut, how to start. Short paragraphs. A list when you are showing what the teacher saw:

- Who was stuck on the same step.
- Who finished without help.
- What the teacher did not have to prepare.

That list is the product. The prose around it should not be longer than the list's usefulness.

## What not to claim

Do not claim you closed a learning gap. Do not claim a teacher's evenings were returned. Do not claim a child "fell in love with reading" unless a parent wrote that, you have permission, and you are willing to leave the sentence as human rather than as a headline. Do not imply a research study. Do not use a student's work as decoration.

Do not stuff the page with the phrase you hope will rank. Name the grade, the skill, and the decision. The reader who needs you can recognize their class without a repeated slogan. The reader who does not need you should be able to leave quickly. That is a successful proof page too.

A note on the stack belongs only if the buyer is choosing a tool their district must host. Most teachers and parents are not. They are choosing a lesson. Keep the engineering quiet unless it protected the learning moment, for example a page that loads fast enough to use on a shared cart of old laptops. Then say that in the constraint, not as a logo row of frameworks.

When the draft still makes sense with the photos removed, the sentences are ready. When it does not, you have a gallery. Add the decision back before you add another frame.

The way people move from this page to a class or a trial is the next design problem. [Navigation for an education product](/blog/navigation-for-an-education-product) should use labels teachers and parents already say, and one path should start the class or the trial. A proof page that is orphaned under "Resources" will not be read by the person who had ten minutes.

If you want the story framed the way a studio frames a project, book [an intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min). Bring the constraint, the screen, and the sentence you are tempted to exaggerate. The call should leave you with a shorter page and a cleaner claim.
